name: Moctezuma II
info: Moctezuma Xocoyotzin (c. 1466–1520), known as Moctezuma II, was the ninth emperor of the Aztec Empire, which reached its greatest size under him, and was its ruler when Hernán Cortés and the Spaniards entered Tenochtitlan in 1519.

facts.born: c. 1466; son of the emperor Axayácatl and a daughter of Nezahualcóyotl, great-grandson of Moctezuma I, and nephew of the emperors Tízoc and Ahuizotl
facts.died: 29 June 1520 in Tenochtitlan, a hostage of the Spaniards; struck by stones from his own people by the Spanish accounts, killed by the Spaniards by indigenous ones
facts.role: Warrior with the ranks of tlacatecuhtli or tlacochcalcatl and main priest of Huitzilopochtli's temple; huey tlatoani (emperor) of the Aztec Empire from 1502 or 1503 to 1520; king consort of Ecatepec through his marriage to Queen Tlapalizquixochtzin
facts.known: the empire's greatest extent, south to Xoconosco and the Isthmus of Tehuantepec; the centralising of government and the widening divide between nobles and commoners; the defeat at Atlixco and the long war with Huejotzingo and Tlaxcala; the meeting with Cortés on 8 November 1519; his captivity and disputed death; the palace zoo and the Chapultepec aqueduct

t: Already a renowned warrior and the main priest of Huitzilopochtli's temple, Moctezuma was elected tlatoani of Mexico in 1502 or 1503 and fought some 73 campaigns, many of them to crush rebellions, carrying the empire to its greatest size.

At home he centralised power in his person, barred commoners from his palace and high office and raised tribute, policies that left subject peoples such as the Totonacs and Chalco ready to ally with Spain.

Received as a guest in 1519 and soon held prisoner in his own palace, he died in June 1520 in circumstances the sources tell differently; Spanish writers later cast him as weak and superstitious, a picture many historians now treat as post-conquest myth.
dyk: A Spanish soldier with Cortés reported that at his meals Moctezuma drank nothing but chocolate, served in a golden goblet, flavoured with vanilla or chili and whipped to a froth.
ev: Born into the Mexica royal house, son of the emperor Axayácatl
Gains the rank of tequihua, earned by capturing at least four enemy commanders
Crowned tlatoani, the year most documents give, though some historians argue for 1503
A major drought begins three years of famine in central Mexico; he raises tribute for a year and orders children sold into slavery for food to be freed
In the year of the New Fire Ceremony his armies conquer Tototepec, Quetzaltepec and other towns in Oaxaca and Guerrero
Secures the election of his nephew Cacamatzin as ruler of Texcoco after Nezahualpilli's death, provoking Ixtlilxochitl's rebellion
Meets Hernán Cortés on the causeway into Tenochtitlan on 8 November and is soon made a prisoner in his own palace
Dies on 29 June during the fighting between the Spaniards and the Mexica after the Massacre in the Great Temple

sections.early:
Moctezuma Xocoyotzin, whose name is read as 'he frowns like a lord', was born around 1466 into the ruling house of the Mexica of Tenochtitlan. He was a son of the emperor Axayácatl and of a daughter of Nezahualcóyotl, the ruler of Texcoco, and a great-grandson of Moctezuma I through his daughter Atotoztli II; the earlier emperors Tízoc and Ahuizotl were his uncles. Xocoyotzin means 'honoured young one', and the regnal number II was given by later historians to tell him from the first Moctezuma.

As was the custom for Mexica nobles, he was educated in the calmecac, the school of the nobility, probably from the age of five. Some sources say he stood out for his discipline and his devotion to the Aztec religion. He made his name in war: under Ahuizotl he led troops to relieve Mexica pochteca merchants besieged during the last stage of the conquest of Ayotlan, and about 1490 he gained the rank of tequihua, reached by capturing at least four enemy commanders. By the time of his election he held the high rank of tlacatecuhtli or tlacochcalcatl in the army and was the main priest of the temple of Huitzilopochtli, and both his military career and his religious standing weighed in his choice as ruler.
sections.rise:
The year of Moctezuma's coronation is uncertain. Most documents give 1502, which most historians accept; others argue for 1503, pointing to the Stone of the Five Suns, whose date 11 Reed corresponds to 15 July 1503, while the chronicler Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxóchitl gives 24 May 1503. His first campaign, held in honour of the coronation, was the violent suppression of a rebellion in Nopala and Icpatepec in Oaxaca, with a force of over 60,000. About 5,100 prisoners were taken, many given as slaves and the rest sacrificed on the fourth day of the coronation; in Nopala the soldiers massacred the inhabitants and burned temples and houses, against his wishes.

At the start of his reign he secretly invited the lords of Tlaxcala, Huexotzinco, Cholula, Michoacan and Metztitlán to his coronation, sending an embassy of experts in diplomacy, espionage and languages, though large wars with these rivals soon followed. To bind the empire to the centre he set up thirty-eight more provincial divisions and sent out officials with garrisons to collect tax, uphold the laws and judge disputes. Many of his early policies were planned with his uncle Tlilpotonqui, the cihuacoatl. He also married Tlapalizquixochtzin, queen of Ecatepec, becoming king consort of that altepetl, a role Bernal Díaz del Castillo says few in Mexico knew of.
sections.deeds:
Moctezuma's reign saw some 73 military engagements before European contact, with victory at about 43 sites, many of them to put down revolts rather than to win new land. His armies pushed into Oaxaca and Guerrero: Achiotlan fell in 1504, Zozollan in 1506, and in 1507, the year of the New Fire Ceremony, Tototepec, Quetzaltepec and other towns, after merchants he had sent were killed. At Tototepec the whole population except the children was massacred; at Tlachquiauhco and later at Jaltepec he ordered all adults over fifty killed to prevent further rebellion. Around 1514 he turned north and east, into the Huastec region, and fought the Tarascan Empire without taking territory. By his reign's end the empire reached as far south as Xoconosco and the Isthmus of Tehuantepec.

At home he faced a drought from 1505 that brought three years of famine. With the lords of Texcoco and Tlacopan he used the food stores to feed the people and raised tribute for a year, and he had the court free the children some nobles had sold as slaves for food. He centralised government in his person: by Alva Ixtlilxóchitl's account he replaced most of his advisers, barred commoners and illegitimate sons of nobles from his palace and high office, and required nobles to live permanently in Tenochtitlan. He built a palace of about 200 by 200 metres, with a famous zoo, the Totocalli, and in 1506 the Chapultepec aqueduct to bring fresh water to the city.
sections.opponents:
Moctezuma's most costly enemies were the states of the Puebla valley. About 1503, or 1507 according to Diego Durán, he provoked a flower war against Huejotzingo and its allies at Atlixco, where his brother or son Tlacahuepan led 100,000 troops and was killed; primary records give about 40,000 dead on both sides, and the defeat was felt as humiliating. Rebellions followed in Oaxaca, and a large series of revolts in 1510 spread too widely for the empire to answer them all. When Tlaxcala overran Huejotzingo, Moctezuma came to Huejotzingo's aid, but a twenty-day battle ended in a standstill, and on 23 September 1519 the Tlaxcalans allied with the Spaniards against him.

His policies made enemies within the empire. Heavier permanent tribute, laid mostly on the Valley of Mexico, drove Totonacapan, Chalco and Mixquic to rebel and later to side with Spain. In 1516 he backed his nephew Cacamatzin for the throne of Texcoco; Ixtlilxochitl, who claimed Moctezuma wanted to rule Texcoco through his nephew, raised an army and besieged the city until the brothers agreed to divide the province. Alva Ixtlilxóchitl went further, calling the affair 'diabolical' and accusing Moctezuma of betraying Nezahualpilli's army to Tlaxcala, a story modern historians generally do not trust. Contemporary judgements of Moctezuma himself were divided: some depict a great conqueror who held his nation together in crisis, others a tyrant seeking absolute control.
sections.last:
Moctezuma learned of Juan de Grijalva's landing on the east coast of the empire in 1518 and posted extra watchtowers. When Hernán Cortés arrived in 1519 he sent emissaries and gifts, and on 8 November met him on the causeway into Tenochtitlan. Cortés wrote that Moctezuma offered at once to cede his realm to Charles V; historians doubt it, noting that his courtly Nahuatl may have meant the opposite of its words, and that Cortés needed such a cession to make war lawful. Soon Moctezuma was a prisoner in his own palace. The Spaniards gave as the reason the killing of Juan de Escalante and about seven Spaniards by the tribute collector Qualpopoca, who was burned; Cortés himself admitted he held Moctezuma mainly to keep control of Mexico.

Moctezuma kept much of his routine but lost most of his power, and he used what remained to protect the Spaniards, having Cacamatzin arrested when he planned an attack. In April 1520, while Cortés was away fighting Pánfilo de Narváez, tensions exploded into the Massacre in the Great Temple, and Moctezuma became a hostage. He died on 29 June 1520. Bernal Díaz says the Spaniards made him speak to his people from a balcony, that the Mexica had chosen his brother Cuitláhuac in his place, and that he was struck by three stones and refused treatment. The Florentine Codex blames the Spaniards; Durán's indigenous informants said Cortés's men stabbed him, and other annals that he was found strangled. Cuitláhuac soon died of smallpox, and Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521.
sections.legacy:
Most of Moctezuma's policies did not survive the conquest, though the divide between nobles and commoners lasted, as the old nobility kept privileges such as land under the cacicazgo in New Spain. His descendants entered both Mexican and Spanish society: his daughter Tecuichpoch became Isabel Moctezuma, and in 1627 his great-grandson Pedro Tesifón de Moctezuma was made Count of Moctezuma, a title raised to a dukedom in 1865. Several indigenous peoples of Mexico worship earth deities named after him, and his name was invoked by rebels against Spanish rule, as in Chiapas in 1721 and by Jacinto Canek, who called himself 'Little Montezuma', in 1761.

His image has been shaped by his role as ruler of a defeated nation. Spanish writers described him as weak-willed, superstitious and indecisive, and the Florentine Codex, compiled about fifty years after the conquest with informants from Tlatelolco, tells of omens and of Cortés taken for the returning god Quetzalcoatl. Matthew Restall counts the belief that superstition left the Aztecs passive among the myths of the conquest, James Lockhart sees Moctezuma made a scapegoat for the defeat, and Anthony Pagden found no preconquest tradition giving Quetzalcoatl that role. Susan Gillespie argues that post-conquest accounts fitted him to the pattern of rulers who closed a dynasty. He is the title figure of operas by Vivaldi, Graun and Mysliveček.

summary: Moctezuma II ruled the Aztec Empire from 1502 or 1503, centralising power in his own person and fighting dozens of campaigns that carried the empire to its greatest extent. His heavy tribute and his long war with Tlaxcala gave the Spaniards allies; held captive by Cortés from 1519, he died in 1520, and his reputation as weak and superstitious is largely a post-conquest construction.

Battle of Atlixco dated 'approximately 1503' or 1507 (Durán); left out of the events list as uncertain, kept in the opponents section with both dates.
Ancestry: the article gives conflicting lines for Huehue Tezozómoc (son of Itzcóatl or of Chimalpopoca); left out.
Death: four versions (Díaz: stones from his people; Florentine Codex: the Spaniards; Durán's indigenous informants: stabbed by Cortés's men; other annals: strangled); all given, none preferred.
The 'some 73 military engagements, victory at about 43 sites' figure is the article's, unattributed.
The Totocalli's alleged feeding with sacrificial victims' bodies left out as hearsay ('allegedly').
